title: Prediction: These 3 Consumer Stocks Will Beat the S&P 500 Over the Next 10 Years
detail:
Prediction: These 3 Consumer Stocks Will Beat the S&P 500 Over the Next 10 Years
Micah Zimmerman, The Motley Fool
Thu, November 26, 2026 at 5:50 PM EST 5 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Beating the S&P 500 sounds simple until you remember how good the index already is, since it has compounded at about 9.9% a year on a total return basis going back to 1928. So a stock that beats the index over 10 years needs more than a good quarter, it needs a business that can keep growing over the long term.

When I look for that kind of staying power in the consumer world, I aim for three things: a brand that people pay up for, a long expansion runway, and a management team that protects both. Here are three consumer stocks that I think long-term investors should consider for the decade ahead.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

1. Ferrari: Fewer cars, more value

Ferrari (NYSE:RACE) deliberately builds fewer cars than people want, and that scarcity is the heart of its economic moat, which is a durable advantage that keeps rivals from stealing its customers.

CEO Benedetto Vigna said in the third-quarter release that deliveries "reflect our clients' ever-deepening desire to make each Ferrari uniquely their own." Those personal touches add profit to every car without adding volume.

Demand isn't the problem. Vigna said on the call, "We continue to experience a healthy demand across all geographies, with an order book that enters 2028."

The risks are a premium valuation, at roughly 36 times earnings, and the shift to electric models like the Luce, which has to win over buyers who love engines.

2. Hilton: Plenty of rooms left to fill

Hilton (NASDAQ:HLT) mostly doesn't own its hotels; it collects fees by managing and licensing its brands to owners through a franchise model, which is an arrangement where a business pays to use another company's brand and systems. That lets it grow without spending heavily on buildings.

CEO Chris Nassetta said in the third-quarter release, "We achieved our highest quarter ever for organic openings." He also said on the call, "Globally, Hilton is still less than 6% of supply providing a long runway for continued growth."

Travel is cyclical, though. CFO Kevin Jacobs said, "RevPAR in China declined 5.4% in the quarter," referring to revenue per available room, which is a key hotel measure of how well rooms are filled and priced. Middle East conflict is weighing on that region, too, and the stock trades near 49 times earnings.

The Nasdaq Composite Is in a Correction, but These 3 Dividend Stocks Are Near 52-Week Highs. Here's Why They're Still Worth Buying Right Now.
Thomas Niel, The Motley Fool
Thu, November 26, 2026 at 4:33 PM EST 5 min read
JNJ
V
^IXIC
^GSPC
NVDA

Trading disclosure

After slumping throughout November, major indexes like the S&P 500 staged something of a comeback on Monday. Tuesday and Wednesday were a bit more chaotic, but the indexes have held onto most of Monday's gains so far. Only time will tell whether this week's action was a dead cat bounce or if it marks the end of the latest stock market pullback. Still, given the recent surge in stocks making new highs, it may be time for investors to consider going defensive.

Across multiple sectors, defensive dividend payers have continued to perform steadily. While each one declined during the sell-off, these three stocks remain near their 52-week highs: Johnson & Johnson (NYSE:JNJ), Coca-Cola (NYSE:KO), and Visa (NYSE:V).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Johnson & Johnson continues its growth pivot

With 64 consecutive years of dividend growth, Johnson & Johnson became one of a small number of Dividend Kings — companies with payout-hiking streaks of 50 years or more — over a decade ago. Yielding around 2% at current prices, this healthcare stock has averaged mid-single-digit annual dividend growth over the past decade.

J&J's latest dividend increase may have only been 3.1%, but the company's ongoing pivot toward a higher-growth business model points to stronger payouts and gains down the road. In particular, the company has pivoted toward building a pipeline of specialty drugs. As Goldman Sachs managing director Asad Haider discussed in an interview with Barron's last month, J&J's recently released drugs include the immunology treatment Tremfya and the psoriasis treatment Icotyde.

Also, per Haider, promising Johnson & Johnson drug candidates include the bladder cancer treatment Inlexa. And recently approved immunology drug Imaavy could generate up to $5 billion in sales. J&J may trade for around 23 times forward earnings, a big premium to other pharmaceutical stocks, but if its growth pivot persists, the stock could sustain or even grow this valuation.

Coca-Cola's growth streak could continue in 2027

Coca-Cola is another Dividend King, with a dividend-growth streak also spanning 64 years. At its current share price, Coca-Cola, one of the world's largest consumer staples companies, has a forward dividend yield of around 2.2%. Its dividend growth has averaged in the mid-single digits in recent years. Still, its strong stock market performance has been driven by its ongoing growth resurgence.

title: Jim Cramer sends strong words to stock market investors
detail:
Jim Cramer sends strong words to stock market investors
Hillary Remy, Dana Sullivan Kilroy
Thu, November 26, 2026 at 4:07 PM EST 6 min read
^GSPC

Most investors check the S&P 500, see a correction, and assume the damage is spread evenly. It isn't. The market has shed roughly $8 trillion since its Oct. 6 peak, but the pain has landed in uneven bursts that can hit one portfolio even harder than the next.

That is what makes a rolling bear so tricky. By the time a sector's slide makes the headlines, the selling has often moved somewhere else.

As Jim Cramer pointed out on a Nov. 17 episode of "Mad Money," "Everyone seems to be reluctant to call this market what it really is: a rolling bear market that's ripping off the faces of everybody," he said.

"It's a rotating bear of a market. It mauls the industrials, then goes after the software stocks, then it hits the hardware, heads for the financials, finds the transports, crushes housing. Sectors can run, but they just can't hide," as reported by 247 Wall St.

Where the bear has already bitten

Look under the hood and it gets uglier. Ron Insana estimates that somewhere between 40% and 50% of S&P 500 companies have fallen at least 20% since market momentum peaked in June. The index itself held up far better than that, which is why so many people are surprised when they open their statements.

Also read: Jim Cramer sees something Wall Street may be missing in Broadcom

Tech has taken the most visible beating. The Nasdaq-100 sank 5.6% on Nov. 20 and came close to bear market territory, as reported by Yahoo Finance. Chipmakers that carried the AI rally suddenly became the stocks everyone wanted to dump first, and the selling spilled into names with little direct AI exposure.

Housing tells a quieter but equally grim story. Builder confidence fell to 25 in November, its lowest level since April 2012, the National Association of Home Builders reported. Nearly half of builders cut prices, and the group's chief economist said mortgage rates above 7% are holding buyers back.

Nvidia is a good example of how fast the mood can swing. The stock jumped 31.48% on Nov. 23 after Jensen Huang was brought back as CEO. Even after that pop, many holders were still underwater after weeks of sharp declines.

Let your mix do the heavy lifting

Jim Cramer says sectors can run but can't hide. That is a pretty good argument against betting everything on one corner of the market. Earlier this year, Vanguard floated the idea that a portfolio with 40% in stocks and 60% in bonds could earn about the same as a classic 60/40 split with less risk.

The firm calls it a concept, not a mandate.

That doesn't mean flipping an allocation overnight. An investor who is sitting at 80% stocks and 20% bonds might only need a modest shift to 70/30, Moneywise reported. Age, goals, and time horizon should drive that decision. And not the latest selloff or the loudest voice on TV.

Walt Disney (NYSE:DIS) closed at $125.60 on Wednesday, November 25, 2026. That was a 2.52% gain from Tuesday's $122.51 close, on a day the S&P 500 slid 0.25%, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.62%.

Josh Hallett / Wikimedia Commons

It was the highest close since April 19, 2022, when shares finished at $131.90. Every close since then has been lower. Disney ended the session with a market value of $214.53 billion, and shares traded at $125.76 after hours at 6:26 p.m. ET.

Real margin and cash flow gains support the rally. However, the stock now trades near the top of its own valuation range, with little room left before it hits the average analyst target.

A Closing High and an Intraday High Worth Separating

Wednesday's milestone counts closing prices only. The intraday peak of $126.28 set a new one-year high, against a low of $92.19. It was also the highest intraday price since August 16, 2022, a different and later date than the closing milestone.

The stock is still 37.8% below its record close of $201.91 on March 8, 2021. It has gained 35.9% from its $92.42 closing low on March 27, 2026.

November's results are not final yet. Shares are up 13.2% from the $110.94 close on October 30. If that gain holds through Monday, November 30, it would be the best month since May 2025, when the stock rose 24.3%.

Warren Buffett's 2026 Thanksgiving message thanks three teachers by name. One is Joe Rosenfield, a Des Moines department store chairman who bought 300 Berkshire Hathaway shares for Grinnell College at 63 for $5,252.

Grinnell sold the shares between 1989 and 1993 for $3.7 million. At this week's price they would be worth about $260 million, about 130 times what the same money earned in the S&P 500.

Rosenfield lived to 96. In the weakest 33-year stretch of the S&P 500 since 1968, about $46,000 set aside at 63 grew to $1 million.

Read: Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps with, and it is free today. Read more here.

Warren Buffett's Thanksgiving message this year thanks three teachers by name, and one of them is a man most investors have never heard of: Joe Rosenfield, a Des Moines businessman who was 63 when he bought 300 shares of Berkshire Hathaway for $5,252. At this week's price those shares would be worth about $260 million.

Rosenfield bought them for Grinnell College, the small Iowa school he graduated from in 1925, and the college no longer owns them. He sold the stake between 1989 and 1993 for $3.7 million. The account comes from Jason Zweig's June 2000 profile of Rosenfield in Money magazine.

Dimitrios Kambouris / Getty Images Entertainment via Getty Images

That sale reads as a warning about letting go of a great business too early, since the shares would now be worth about 70 times what Grinnell got for them; it is also hindsight, and Rosenfield's other choices still took the college's endowment from $11 million to more than $1 billion. Zweig reported that neither Rosenfield, Buffett nor anyone at Grinnell could recall the reason for the sale.

What Buffett wrote this Thanksgiving

Berkshire released the message on Nov. 16, along with news that Buffett, who is 96 and now chairman emeritus, had given 9,225,000 Class B shares to four family foundations.

HP (NYSE:HPQ) rose $3.21, or 11.49%, to $31.15 on Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. That was the biggest gain of any S&P 500 stock. It came in a session when the index fell 0.25%, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.62%.

Justin Sullivan / Getty Images

It was HP's best day since May 22, 2026, when the stock gained 15.25%. It was also the highest close since Oct. 29, when the stock finished at $31.83. Volume reached 39.1 million shares, up from 27.1 million on Tuesday.

That close puts the stock ahead of most of Wall Street. The 18 analysts covering HP rate it a Hold on average, and their average one-year target is $27.55. HP now trades about 13% above that level. Several firms raised their targets after the report and still rate the stock a sell.

Guidance Slightly Above Consensus Brought In Buyers

HP reported after the close on Nov. 24. Fiscal fourth-quarter revenue was $16.0 billion, up 9.3%, and non-GAAP EPS was $0.83. Fiscal 2027 non-GAAP EPS guidance is $3.15 to $3.45.

HPQ Earnings Explorer — 24/7 Wall St.

The $3.30 midpoint sits a little above the $3.28 FactSet consensus, which likely explains much of the buying. HP also raised its quarterly dividend to $0.31 from $0.30. The new rate is payable Jan. 6, 2027 to holders of record on Dec. 9, 2026.
